title: Piano Concerto No. 3 in C minor
hook: A quiet drumbeat Beethoven planned in 1796 waits at the heart of his stormiest concerto.

painting.title: Landscape with Hammer Mill
painting.pairingNote: Painted in Vienna around 1800, while the concerto was taking shape; a forge glows in a dark valley, its hammer beating like the drum in the music, under a sky breaking into light.

facts: Beethoven noted the first idea in 1796, on a concert tour that took him to Berlin, and probably hoped to play the concerto in Vienna in April 1800. It was not ready. The premiere came on 5 April 1803 at the Theater an der Wien, with Beethoven as soloist, in a concert that also introduced his Second Symphony and the oratorio *Christ on the Mount of Olives*.

Even then the solo part was not fully written down. His page-turner, Ignaz von Seyfried, later recalled pages that were almost empty apart from a few scribbled signs: Beethoven played most of it from memory.
It is Beethoven’s only piano concerto in a minor key, and its C minor drama owes something to Mozart’s Concerto K. 491 in the same key.
One of the very first ideas he wrote down was “kettledrum at the cadenza”. It became the quiet, mysterious ending of the first movement, where the timpani and the piano talk softly together.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a contest between piano and orchestra (I), a slow song in a far-away key (II), a restless dance that breaks into C major (III).

movements.heading: Allegro con brio
movements.summary: The orchestra plays for more than three minutes before the piano says a word. Then the soloist storms in and goes through the same themes again, its own way: the Classical [[double-exposition|double exposition]]. After the [[cadenza|cadenza]] comes the moment Beethoven planned first of all, a soft dialogue of piano and kettledrum.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: quiet strings in unison climb the notes of the C minor chord, then a short knocking rhythm answers. The knock returns all through the movement.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a gentle, singing melody in the major, in violins and clarinets.

stops.hear: Strings alone, soft and in unison, climb a C minor chord; a short knocking rhythm answers
stops.happening: Theme 1. The orchestra begins the [[exposition|exposition]] on its own

stops.hear: The whole orchestra bursts out loudly with the same theme
A soft, singing melody in violins and clarinets
The piano enters with three rising scales, then strikes the theme in octaves
The piano takes over the singing melody and decorates it
After an orchestral outburst, the piano comes back with its rising scales, but in a bright, unexpected key
stops.happening: The [[development|development]] begins, in D major. Much of it is quiet

stops.hear: The opening theme returns, loud, in the full orchestra
The orchestra stops on a held chord; the piano plays alone, free and stormy
Instead of a loud orchestral close: the piano very soft, and the kettledrum tapping the knocking rhythm

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Rising scales again; the orchestra gathers strength
stops.happening: A firm ending in C minor

notice: Listen to how long the orchestra plays before the piano’s first note. The piano’s three scales sound like a door thrown open.
After the cadenza, follow the timpani. It plays the knocking rhythm of the first bars, now almost a whisper.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Richter and Kurt Sanderling had already played this concerto together in Moscow in 1952, and Sanderling recorded it again in 1994 with Mitsuko Uchida (see the other recommendations). On the Spotify album the concerto is tracks 4–6, after Mozart’s D minor Concerto.

movements.heading: Largo
movements.summary: After C minor, Beethoven jumps to E major, a key very far away. The effect is like stepping into another room. The piano begins alone with a slow, hymn-like melody in soft chords; the orchestra answers.

mainIdeas.name: The Largo melody
mainIdeas.description: slow, quiet chords in the piano, with the tune on top.

mainIdeas.name: The middle section
mainIdeas.description: the piano’s flowing [[arpeggio|arpeggio]]s under a duet of flute and bassoon.

stops.hear: The piano alone: soft chords, a slow melody on top
stops.happening: The theme, in E major, far from C minor

stops.hear: The orchestra enters softly and continues the song
The piano sings again, now with fine runs and ornaments
The piano ripples quietly; above it, flute and bassoon sing to each other
The opening melody returns in the piano
The piano alone for a few moments, free and expressive

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: A last quiet echo of the theme, then one sudden loud chord from the whole orchestra

notice: The last chord. After ten minutes of soft music, it is the loudest sound in the movement.

movements.heading: Rondo. Allegro
movements.summary: A [[rondo|rondo]]: the piano’s nervous C minor tune keeps coming back, with brighter episodes in between. Near the end the music switches to a quick, lilting six-beat dance, and C minor turns into C major.

mainIdeas.name: The rondo tune
mainIdeas.description: quick and restless, with a leaning, accented note right at its start.

mainIdeas.name: Episode 1
mainIdeas.description: a carefree tune in the major, first in E-flat major, later in C major.

mainIdeas.name: Episode 2
mainIdeas.description: a calm clarinet melody, followed by a passage in which the strings enter one after another.

stops.hear: The piano alone plays a quick, nervous tune
The whole orchestra takes the tune up loudly
A carefree tune in the piano, in the major
The nervous tune returns in the piano
A clarinet sings a calm melody; the piano answers
The strings enter one by one on the same short tune

stops.label: After the fugato
stops.hear: The tune drifts into a distant, brighter key before finding its way home
stops.happening: A glance back at E major, the key of the Largo

stops.hear: The carefree tune again, now in C major
stops.happening: Episode 1 returns in the home key

stops.hear: The beat changes to a quick, swinging six; everything is in C major

stops.label: Last seconds
stops.hear: Loud, bright C major chords

notice: Listen to the accented, leaning note at the start of the rondo tune. On the piano it is the same key as the G-sharp at the heart of the Largo’s E major chord, written as A-flat. Beethoven uses it as a hinge between the two movements.

threads.title: A drum from 1796
threads.body: The first idea Beethoven wrote down was a kettledrum after the cadenza. Its knocking rhythm runs through the first movement and gets the last, quietest word.

threads.title: Minor to major
threads.body: The first movement ends firmly in C minor; the finale breaks out into a C major dash.

threads.title: A far-away key
threads.body: The Largo’s E major is a world apart, and the finale’s leaning note keeps a thread back to it.
